articles.headline: Bournemouth enjoy night to remember as 10-man Milan fail to weather storm
keyFacts: Bournemouth defeated AC Milan in a dominant home match that featured a penalty and a red card for Milan goalkeeper Mike Maignan.
Manager Marco Rose said Bournemouth suffocated their opponents and praised his team's brilliant performance from the first minute to the last.
Bournemouth will next play an away match against Manchester United on Sunday.
body: This was a momentous night in Bournemouth’s history, although the truth is they would have been given a far sterner examination by Coventry or Hull. Whatever this rotten impersonation of a Milan side was, it bore no relation to those that forged such a celebrated history. The visitors resembled holograms even before their goalkeeper Mike Maignan, with an extraordinary rush of blood resulting in a penalty and red card, rendered their task impossible. They never showed the slightest hint of putting up a fight.

Bournemouth simply swamped the seven-time European champions and, amid a swirling south coast storm that rarely let up, could depart singing in the rain. Amine Adli’s sumptuous late free-kick, curled left-footed from 22 yards, meant they could finish the evening with the flourish they deserved. Their joy was clear at full time and met disapproval from some of Milan’s staff, who appeared to take umbrage in a short-lived fracas near the tunnel afterwards.

It was certainly an abject return to English soil for Ruben Amorim, who could have been excused in seeing this particular week as the opportunity to prove a point. Amorim may view Bournemouth as kryptonite given they beat his Manchester United side by an identical scoreline at Old Trafford in December 2024. As it happens that is where the Cherries head on Sunday. On this damning evidence the modern version of Milan share more than a few similarities with his former employers.

“A difficult night in every aspect,” Amorim said. It began with a downpour and waves of Bournemouth pressure, an incisive move ending with Justin Kluivert missing his kick and Ben Gannon-Doak’s drive deflecting wide. Milan failed to clear their lines from the resulting corner and were punished when VAR found Koni De Winter had deflected Evanilson’s header wide with his arm. Kluivert converted the spot kick coolly and the die was firmly cast.

Amorim’s attempt to divide the match into two parts, before and after Maignan’s 27th-minute dismissal, cut no ice. Bournemouth’s tempo had been far too much for Milan before that, Maignan saving untidily from Ryan Christie after Yunus Musah’s pocket had been picked. “We just suffocated them, we didn’t give anything to them,” said a satisfied Marco Rose. “The way they did it today was just brilliant from the first minute until the last.”

When Maignan clawed James Hill’s deflected shot wide, everybody on view set up for a left-sided corner. Nobody was prepared for Maignan, who perhaps expected to be manhandling a taller opponent, to shove Tyler Adams in the face as the ball was sent in. It was a moment of supreme idiocy from the captain; the penalty award was inevitable and so, even before confirmation via VAR, was his departure. This time Marcus Tavernier did the honours, beating the replacement keeper Lorenzo Torriani.

Barely half an hour in, the outcome had been settled. Bournemouth could hardly have imagined, in making their “great escape” from the fourth-tier trapdoor in 2009, that they might land in such a position against Italian royalty. Past luminaries looked on from the stands, Harry Redknapp among them, while their polished successors turned the screw down below.

The relentless Gannon-Doak, called “a special player” afterwards by Rose, thrilled and frustrated in equal measure; the substitute Rayan almost set up a goal for Christie with a delightful piece of skill. It was Adli, another replacement, who applied a delicate garnish.

What a night, then, for a club that knows what it is to gaze into the abyss. “How did we end up here?” asked the public address announcer before kick-off, a question repeated on a banner hoisted by the Steve Fletcher Stand, but it was worth posing in a different sense too. The sizable elephant in the room was how the Premier League’s 15th-placed team could face down one of Serie A’s most decorated institutions, unbeaten domestically this season, and simply sweep them off the park.

In truth nobody could feign too much surprise; certainly not the bookmakers, who deemed Bournemouth the pre-match favourites. Scoffing at Milan’s inadequacy is, up to a point, simply plucking low-hanging fruit. Football’s ecosystem has arrived in a glum place where outwardly fairytale occasions like this are packaged with caveats: even the English top flight’s relative minnows are, through financial and physical power, playing on a different pitch to representatives of leagues once deemed its equals.
For those understandably immersed in the here and now, Rayan came close to a superb fourth. “I’m happy for our fans especially,” Rose said. It is unlikely to be Bournemouth’s last European gala show.

articles.headline: A new subscription service promises an evolving collection of 'bold and bizarre' indie games
keyFacts: Publisher Pantaloon launched a new $5-per-month subscription service called the Playbill featuring experimental indie games.
Founder Jamin Smith said the service will not feature any games that use generative AI in any form.
The initial lineup includes 13 third-party and first-party titles, with games cycling out when key supplies run out.
body: A new subscription service promises an evolving collection of 'bold and bizarre' indie games
Publisher Pantaloon says the Playbill won't feature games that use generative AI in any way.

Curator-turned-publisher Pantaloon has unleashed a subscription service that fans of indie games might be interested in digging into. The Playbill is a take on Xbox Game Pass, albeit one that focuses on "bold and bizarre" titles.

The initial lineup features third-party games such as Buckshot Roulette, Silt, Ex Sanguis and Cabin Factory. Those sit alongside Pantaloon's own games: Sub-Verge, Occlude, It Takes a War, Boxroom, Rolla and the delightful music creation sim Offbeat.

Much like Game Pass offers first-party Xbox titles (save for new Call of Duty offerings) to subscribers on day one, the Playbill will gain all of Pantaloon's own games as soon as they're released. The service even has its own timed exclusive in the shape of Virtue: Prologue, a visual novella companion piece for Virtue and a Sledgehammer, which is out next week (and a game I'm very much looking forward to.

In addition, the Playbill offers demos, playtests and "abandoned prototypes" for you to check out in a section called the Green Room. At the outset, there are playtests for a few interesting-looking games, namely Isle Goblin, Mr Magpie's Harmless Card Game and Lemonade Apocalypse.

"We want the Playbill to be a celebration of more experimental and eccentric games," Pantaloon founder Jamin Smith said. "The nature of the model reduces that barrier to entry for players to check out genres and experiences that might not be surfaced by Steam's market-shaping algorithms. It's also worth stating that we won't feature or platform any games that use genAI in any form; the Playbill is a celebration of the craft of making games."

Pantaloon moved into publishing after building an audience of more than 50,000 newsletter subscribers, who were able to complete puzzles to receive game keys or pay for codes for its curated titles. The puzzles are free to access on the Playbill, along with the service's community features, Virtue: Prologue and a couple of ARGs. The full lineup of games is available through a Primo subscription, which costs a reasonable $5 per month or $60 per year.

It's worth noting that the service is key-based. Pantaloon will cycle games out of the Playbill when it runs out of keys and it will add new titles on a regular basis. Annual subscribers can snag all 13 games in the initial lineup, as well as each new title that's introduced.

Things are different for monthly subscribers. They'll get a guaranteed game each month, and they won't be able to pick which one. "The monthly titles are part of bespoke partnerships, so the games are defined," Smith told Engadget. "That said, some of our puzzles — like this month's — allow a choice of reward to those that can solve."

If you sign up for a monthly plan, you'll be able to access all of the games after you've been a subscriber for six consecutive months. This is "a mechanism just to prevent somebody getting all 14 titles straight away and then canceling," Smith added.

articles.headline: Sony Continues Its March Towards An All-Digital Future As It Reportedly Kills Off Its Last 4K UHD Player
keyFacts: Sony Japan has discontinued its last remaining 4K UHD Blu-ray player, the UBP-X700/K, according to reports and the company website.
The change reflects Sony's broader trend of reducing investments in physical media and hardware production, such as selling TV factories to TCL.
Physical media fans are concerned that Sony's move signals a broader transition toward an all-digital future.
body: It seems that Sony is exiting the UHD Blu-ray market, as it reportedly has quietly discontinued its one remaining 4K UHD player. It’s part of a larger change at Sony that has seen the electronics and entertainment giant investing less and less in hardware and physical media over the last year or so. And it has fans of physical media nervous.
As first spotted by FlatpanelsHD, the Japanese blog and electronics reseller Kunkoku claimed that sales for the UBP-X700/K are officially ending on October 22 in Japan.

This was the last remaining UHD player manufactured and sold by Sony in Japan. This means that, at least locally, the only new UHD player from the company that will be available is the PlayStation 5. The last major electronics company still making UHD players is now Panasonic. Sony is also, for now at least, still making one DVD player model and one Blu-ray player model.
'Sony reportedly exits UHD Blu-ray player market' https://t.co/WSUgXtk6RJ
'Sony Japan has discontinued its last remaining UHD Blu-ray player, UBP-X700/K, seemingly marking the company's exit.
The news comes via Japanese blog Kunkoku, which happens to also be a Sony retailer.â¦ pic.twitter.com/ZEb1zWA1IK
— Wario64 (@Wario64) October 22, 2026

On Sony Japan’s website, the company lists the UBP-X700/K UHD 4K player as being “Out of stock,” with the added message that “This item will not be restocked,” seemingly confirming Kunkoku’s report. We don’t yet know if Sony intends to globally stop production on the X700/K player, but historically, what happens in Japan tends to be a preview of the company’s larger plans for the rest of the world. So it seems very likely that soon, Sony will be completely done making dedicated UHD players for consumers.

This seems to be connected to Sony divesting from electronics production. Earlier this year, Sony sold off much of its TV and hardware production factories and facilities to TCL as part of a larger deal that also saw TCL take a controlling stake in Sony’s Bravia TV business. Also earlier this year, Sony announced its plan to end PlayStation disc production in 2028.

All of this points to a harsh reality for fans who like to own physical copies of movies and games: That future is likely on the way out as companies look to move toward an all-digital future. Hold on to your discs, folks. Things are going to get rough out there.

articles.headline: PHP2Shell exploit bypasses protections designed to stop remote code execution
keyFacts: VulnCheck researchers developed an exploit that bypasses Address Space Layout Randomization to achieve remote code execution via the PHP2Shell vulnerability.
The PHP Foundation disclosed and issued patches for the critical bugs, identified as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, on Wednesday.
VulnCheck warned that organizations should prioritize patching rather than relying on existing memory protections or configuration changes to stop attacks.
body: Researchers have developed a new exploit that shows how even Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) on an x86-64 server cannot stop the PHP2Shell vulnerability. VulnCheck, which made it available to only the company’s Initial Access Intelligence customers, also warned that threat actors are using AI to find even more ways to attack.

The team told us that it’s a “significant advance” because up until now, ASLR has been a major barrier to exploiting PHP2Shell on real-world servers. They don't expect that to hold, though. “Adversaries are clearly spending time (and tokens) on this bug,” Spencer McIntyre, director of exploit development at VulnCheck, told The Register .
The PHP2Shell mess grew even bigger on Thursday amid reports of attackers abusing the security flaws days before they were disclosed and UK government websites proactively going dark.

Vulncheck's exploit targets CVE-2026-109618 , a critical, out-of-memory corruption bug that leads to remote code execution (RCE) in PHP, and part of the PHP2Shell pair alongside CVE-2026-109619 . The PHP Foundation officially disclosed and issued patches for both on Wednesday.

Overnight, VulnCheck researchers developed what they believe is the first known exploit to achieve remote code execution on ASLR-enabled x86-64 systems with PHP's recommended production configuration.

ASLR is a built-in defense against memory-corruption bugs – like PHP2Shell – that randomly arranges memory locations of a program's key data areas. By scrambling these components live, in memory every time a program runs, ASLR prevents an attacker trying to achieve RCE from correctly guessing the target memory address – and thus prevents them from executing malicious code.
While VulnCheck has seen “hundreds” of PHP2Shell proof-of-concept repositories on GitHub, “very few contain legitimate, working exploits,” McIntyre told us, adding that this is largely due to ASLR.

“There's a significant difference between demonstrating a vulnerability and developing an exploit that can overcome the security protections found in real-world environments,” McIntyre said. “One of the biggest obstacles has been ASLR, a protection designed to make memory corruption vulnerabilities much harder to exploit.”

The threat hunters’ new technique, we’re told, bypasses ASLR. It uses a confirmed memory leak chained into RCE on PHP 8.4.26, and they claim it works on x86-64 platforms even with ASLR enabled and PHP’s recommended display_errors=off production configuration.

“We haven't identified another public or commercial exploit that achieves this under the same conditions,” McIntyre said. “Developing this capability was far from trivial, but it demonstrates that a major barrier to exploiting PHP2Shell on production-configured systems can be overcome.”
VulnCheck says it also works on ARM64, but the RCE is not currently functional on ARM-based systems.

This should be a wake-up call to all organizations that, especially now in the era of AI bug hunting and exploit development , “the technical difficulty of exploiting a vulnerability shouldn't be confused with protection against it,” McIntyre said.
“Organizations running vulnerable versions of PHP should prioritize patching rather than assume existing memory protections or configuration changes will stop an attack.” ®

articles.headline: How to find Weapon Manuals in Modern Warfare 4 DMZ
keyFacts: Players in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 DMZ can find rare Weapon Manuals inside Safes and Military Containers located in red-marked High Threat Areas.
Found manuals must be moved to an Insured Slot to guarantee they remain in the player's inventory even without a successful extraction.
Weapon Manuals can be used at the Gunsmith to unlock new weapons and provide permanent inventory access.
body: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 ‘s DMZ mode has switched the old system that revolved around weapons. This year, there are different ways to unlock weapons, and one of the most consistent methods is to gather Weapon Manuals.
However, these items are extremely rare to find and get, and I will explain the method in this guide.
Table of contents
How to get Weapon Manuals in Modern Warfare 4 DMZ
How to use Weapon Manuals in Modern Warfare 4 DMZ
How to get Weapon Manuals in Modern Warfare 4 DMZ

There’s no definite or fixed way to obtain Weapon Manuals since it all depends on your luck. There are two loot sources that can reward you with these items: Safes and Military Containers (Weapon Lockers).

Look for loot that you can find in High Threat Areas. If you don’t know where these regions are, open the tac-map. High Threat Areas are always marked in red. If you’re completing any Operations, you should finish them first.

Image via Activision Once you’re at the correct areas, it’s all about your luck next. If you manage to find a Manual, your first task is to move it to your Insured Slot. You can only use Weapon Manuals if you manage to bring them back safely. Hence, the Insured Slot is a guarantee for it to remain in your inventory even if you don’t manage to extract safely.
How to use Weapon Manuals in Modern Warfare 4 DMZ

Once you manage to get a Weapon Manual, you can then use it to unlock new weapons at the Gunsmith. While they’re immensely useful, there are other methods to get new weapons in the mode. All blueprints that you unlock will also unlock the corresponding weapon for you.
Similarly, all weapons in your inventory when you extract will be available for you to pick from. That said, Weapon Manuals adds permanence to your inventory when it comes to unlocking new weapons.

articles.headline: Disgraced eMudhra drops out of TLS business after using cert private key of 4
keyFacts: Certificate authority eMudhra is withdrawing from the global TLS business following the issuance of eight defective credentials with extremely weak private keys.
V. Srinivasan, chairman of eMudhra Limited, cited increasing compliance costs, low revenue contribution, and disproportionate social media scrutiny as reasons for the decision.
Researchers revealed that the compromised certificates had key sizes ranging from 3 to 8 bits, allowing anyone to easily crack them and generate trusted TLS certificates.
body: eMudhra, the certificate authority that issued eight intermediate TLS credentials so weak that anyone could mint certificates for any website or mail server—one had a private encryption key of just 4—said it’s getting out of the business.

V. Srinivasan, chairman of India-based eMudhra Limited, cited increasing costs and complexities of compliance requirements—paired with the business generating just 1 percent of its revenue. He also said that the emergence of organizations providing TLS certificates free of charge further reduced returns on investment when compared to other products and services the company offers.
Don’t let the door hit you on the butt

“However, the level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” the company continued in a Thursday post. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.”

The announcement came two days after researchers revealed eMudhra had issued eight certificates with private keys so defective they were trivial to discover. Anyone who took the time—which was measured in milliseconds—could crack them and then use them to generate TLS certificates that would be trusted by all major browsers, as well as an untold number of email servers, IoT devices, Docker containers, forgotten Linux machines, and unmaintained CLI tools that ship their own copy of the roots.

Whereas NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private keys—used in the type of certificates eMudhra issued—are supposed to contain roughly 384 bits of entropy, the eight compromised certificates had key sizes ranging from 3 to 8 bits. Stated differently, whereas there are supposed to be 2384—a number with 116 digits—different key possibilities, the strongest of the defective keys had a maximum of just 256. The private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237.

articles.headline: Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax
keyFacts: Meta agreed to a new stock deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to keep him from leaving California over a proposed state billionaire tax.
The agreement provides Zuckerberg with more Meta shares and quarterly selling rights to offset potential personal losses from a one-time 5% state tax.
Meta stated the eight-year deal is critically important to maintain Zuckerberg's leadership in California during ongoing industry transformations related to artificial intelligence.
body: - Published
Meta has agreed to a new deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to prevent him from leaving California over a proposed state tax on billionaires.

The agreement gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn (Â£149bn), even more shares in Meta to make up for the fraction of his fortune he may lose if the tax wins voter approval in November.
The measure would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents with a net worth of more than $1bn. It would likely see the Facebook co-founder pay around $10bn in additional state taxes.
He secured the deal with a special committee of Meta after "robust" and "at several points, contentious" negotiations, according to a Wednesday financial disclosure.
California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group.
The wealth of such people, including Zuckerberg, has ballooned in recent years. Meanwhile, his estimated effective tax rate in California was less than 1%, external each year.

Nevertheless, Zuckerberg told Meta's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California, and even selling his property in the state. His main homes in Californa are in Palo Alto and Lake Tahoe.
Such a move "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees", Zuckerberg told the board.
It would also "raise questions for management of the company going forward", he claimed.
In response, Meta decided to create more shares of stock in the company in order to give Zuckerberg a way to essentially make up any wealth he may lose through the tax proposal.

Through what's known as a stock split announced by the company on Wednesday, Meta created an entirely new type of stock and gave one new share to each existing shareholder. Zuckerberg is one of the company's largest shareholders and famously controls the company through the design of his holdings.

Through the deal, he will receive more stock, more often, and also be able to sell it on a quarterly basis, according to the company's financial filing. The shares will not change his level control over Meta, but they will allow him to cash in more easily on the company's value.
The deal appears to be effective even if the one-time tax in California does not pass, and will go on for eight years - as long as Zuckerberg remains a resident of California.
'Critically important'

Meta called the deal with Zuckerberg its "Founder Alignment Agreement," saying it was "critically important" to keep him leading the company from California given the "dramatic and unprecedented transformation taking place in the tech industry and global economy related to artificial intelligence."
The company alluded to problems the company experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Zuckerberg began working outside of the office and mostly from his large compound in Kauai, Hawaii.

After a surge in hiring at Meta during the pandemic, a whistleblower scandal that led to renewed focus on child safety, and a refocus within the company to building out the "metaverse," which included renaming the company Meta from Facebook, the company began mass layoffs and restructuring.
Layoffs have continued into this year. The company's headcount is down 15% from a year ago, meaning it has shed at least 10,000 workers.
Today, the company has moved away from the "metaverse," or virtual platforms, and is more focused on artificial intelligence products and related tools.
With Zuckerberg leading the company's efforts to catch up in the AI race, Meta's board said it sees a future of "tremendous market opportunity" for the company.
Major tech companies are set to spend an estimated $1 trillion, external this year alone developing AI and the costly infrastructure around it, like data centres.
Meta said on Wednesday it planned to spend as much as $145bn this year on AI projects. The company has increased the amount it expects to spend on AI each financial quarter so far this year.

It is spending so much on the technology that it posted negative cash flow for the first time since the company went public 14 years ago. Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Meta is now spending more money than it is bringing in.

And the company intends to spend even more in the year ahead. Susan Li, Meta's chief financial officer, said on Wednesday that another benefit of the stock split would be to give the company more ways to finance future spending on AI work.
The degree of the company's spending on AI, without an clear new revenue stream coming from it, appeared to spook investors on Thursday.
Meta's shares fell more than 7%, wiping more than $100bn off of the company's market capitalisation, a key metric used worldwide to measure the value of a publicly-traded company.

articles.headline: Trump pushback, Biden 'disaster' and gender surprise: 5 key moments from Kansas Senate debate
keyFacts: Republican Senator Roger Marshall and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton debated in Kansas as both parties compete for U.S. Senate control.
Both candidates addressed personal controversies involving unpaid medical bills and handling church camp abuse allegations.
Hamilton called Biden's border policies a disaster, while Marshall noted he does not always agree with President Trump.
body: Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton sparred over President Donald Trump, immigration, Iran, transgender athletes, artificial intelligence and personal controversies during a contentious Kansas Senate debate Wednesday night.

The hourlong showdown came less than two weeks before Election Day as Marshall seeks a second term and Hamilton, a longtime pastor, tries to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas since 1932.

The race has drawn increased national attention as Republicans and Democrats battle for control of the Senate, with Trump traveling to Kansas earlier this week to campaign for Marshall — a topic touched on during the debate.
Here are five moments that stood out from Wednesday night's debate.
SLEEPER SENATE RACE EMERGES AS UNEXPECTED HEADACHE FOR REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS
The debate wasted little time getting contentious, opening with questions about controversies that have fueled attacks against both candidates.
Marshall was confronted with a New York Times review that found his former medical practice sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills.
"Every year we gave away $3 to $4 million of charity, but we also had a business," Marshall responded. "We had 300 employees, we had a mortgage payment, we had electric."
Hamilton, meanwhile, was questioned about his handling of allegations involving a volunteer at his church's summer camp who was accused of sexual abuse.
Hamilton acknowledged that he should have ensured the individual did not return to the camp following an initial investigation.
FROM 'THIRD REICH' TO ‘NOT THAT INFORMED’: SENATE DEBATES DELIVER FIREWORKS BEFORE MIDTERMS
"I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back," Hamilton said. "That was a mistake on my part."
Trump became part of the debate after moderators played footage from the president's campaign appearance for Marshall in Kansas earlier in the week.
"And at this election, I'm asking you to pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot. Just pretend," Trump told the crowd.
Marshall was then asked whether Trump's support meant Kansans should expect him to back every part of the president's agenda.
"No," Marshall responded, saying there had been "multiple times" when he objected to Trump.
Pressed to identify a specific disagreement, Marshall pointed to recent immigration enforcement in southwest Kansas and Trump's approach to beef imports .
"Just like with my wife, I can disagree with her. My wife is always right," Marshall joked. "And President Trump is not always right."
Marshall nevertheless urged Trump voters to turn out for him, arguing that electing Hamilton could help Democrats capture the Senate.
The two rivals found themselves in agreement when the moderator asked each candidate how many genders there are.
"There's two. There's a boy and there's a girl," Marshall said. "I delivered 5,000 of them and almost half were boys and half were girls."
"There are two genders, male and female ," Hamilton responded.
TOP TAKEAWAYS FROM JD VANCE TOWN HALL: COSTLY GAS, DC CORRUPTION, IMMIGRATION HOT TAKES AND THE WAR
The candidates then turned to the debate over transgender participation in women's sports .
Hamilton said decisions over athletic eligibility should generally be made locally but was unequivocal about whether biological males should compete against females.
"I have a 12-year-old granddaughter. I don't want biological men or boys competing against her that could harm her," Hamilton said. "It's not a fair, fair fight."
Marshall argued that by high school, "boys need to be in boys sports, girls in girls sports," while accusing national Democrats of pushing "transgender ideology."
Hamilton later accused Marshall of using the issue to "pick on" and "bully" people.
Hamilton called for greater federal oversight of artificial intelligence and compared the emerging technology to the development of nuclear power and nuclear weapons.
"We developed a Nuclear Regulatory Commission. We need to do the same thing with AI," Hamilton said.
But when the moderator pressed him to identify specific federal regulations he would support, Hamilton acknowledged he did not yet have an answer.
"You know what? I'm not sure, to be honest," Hamilton said, arguing that even experts are struggling to understand the technology's potential dangers.

Marshall advocated a "light touch" approach focused on national security, transparency, protecting children and privacy, while slamming a one-size-fits-all global order for artificial intelligence advancement.
Hamilton pushed back sharply.
"This is an existential — potential existential threat to the human race," Hamilton said. "We can't just go with a light touch and hope everybody does their best."
BIDEN CONSPICUOUSLY ABSENT FROM CAMPAIGN TRAIL AS OBAMA, HARRIS STEP UP FOR MIDTERM PUSH
Hamilton sought to put distance between himself and former President Joe Biden when moderators challenged the Democrat over his claim that he would "lead from the middle."

The moderator pointed to Hamilton's past donations to Democrats, including Biden, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kan., before asking him to identify a progressive policy he opposed.
"The Biden policies when it came to the border were a disaster," Hamilton responded. "I believe in strong and secure borders."
"I'm not somebody who favors the Socialist Party," Hamilton added. "I'm somebody who stands in the middle."
Hamilton also reiterated during the debate that he would not support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer for majority leader if Democrats capture control of the chamber.

articles.headline: U.S. reducing troop footprint in Middle East, sources say
keyFacts: Brent crude oil prices surged about 3% to $112 per barrel after Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed it attacked vessels near the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi authorities reported that an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed two people and injured eight others.
Sources told CBS News that the U.S. military is reducing its troop footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats and attacks.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:

- The price of Brent crude oil surged about 3% Thursday to $112 per barrel as Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it had attacked four vessels near the Strait of Hormuz for using a route that Tehran rejects. The IRGC said three other ships using that route hit sea mines and were forced to halt.

- The U.S. military has at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats and attacks by Iran and its in Yemen, sources told CBS News on Wednesday. The latest attack, on King Fahd International Airport in the eastern Saudi city of Dammam, has killed at least two people and injured eight more.

- Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday that indirect negotiations with the U.S. continue over a seven-day ceasefire proposal that President Trump last month, with the U.S. seeking new clauses.
Iran's shadow fleet tankers have run out of oil, intelligence firm tells Wall Street Journal

The shadow fleet of tankers holding Iran's offshore oil reserves, which it had been selling to China throughout the war against the U.S. and Israel, have run dry, intelligence firm Kpler told The Wall Street Journal on Wednesday.

The millions of barrels of crude, held on dozens of oil tankers in Asian water, ran out in mid-October, Kpler told the outlet, with a U.S. naval blockade preventing Iran from replacing the crude being sold to Chinese refineries.
"There's no more oil to discharge to China anymore," said Homayoun Falakshahi, head of crude-oil analysis at the firm.
The U.S. naval blockade has cost Iran at least $25 billion in oil revenue, according to U.S. Central Command.
Egypt urges political solution between Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthis
Egypt's Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty on Thursday said all options must be explored to find a political solution between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.
At a press conference where he reiterated solidarity with Saudi Arabia, he stressed "the necessity of exploring all avenues for reaching political solutions."
The conflict between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government and the Iran-backed Houthis erupted in summer and has drastically escalated in recent weeks.
Egypt announced Sunday that it was prepared to provide military assistance to Saudi Arabia.
CBS/AFP
Houthis claim Saudi Arabia targeted an Indian yacht in the Red Sea
A spokesman for Yemen's Houthi rebels accused Saudi Arabia on Thursday of targeting an Indian yacht near Zuqar Island in the Red Sea with 14 Indian nationals on board.
In a statement published on X, Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the group's forces were carrying out rescue operations and would provide further information later.
"The Saudi enemy targets an Indian yacht near Zuqar Island, with 14 people of Indian nationality on board, according to preliminary information," he wrote in his post.

"This reckless act by the Saudi enemy in targeting the yacht threatens international navigation in the Red Sea, and the international community must stop the Saudi enemy from these reckless actions," said Saree.
There was no further information or other reports available to corroborate the Houthis' claim.
Iran's army chief says country is ready for asymmetrical warfare
The Commander-in-Chief of the Iranian Army, Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami, said Thursday that the country's armed forces were prepared for asymmetric warfare and satisfied with their drone capacity.

"In the previous asymmetric war, we fought the enemy with equipment that surprised them, as they received very heavy blows," he said, referring to the intense exchange of fire with the U.S. and Israel before a June ceasefire was announced. That deal, which President , failed to bring about the negotiations on Iran's nuclear program and many other issues that it provisioned, but neither side has engaged in major strikes since the summer, with fighting in the region largely shifting to the linked conflict in Yemen.
"We have reached a good level of maturity in the field of drones and unmanned systems," Hatami said. "We assure our dear people of Iran that we are in a good position."
Top European, Mideast diplomats to meet in Istanbul Friday, AFP reports

Top European diplomats will hold talks in Istanbul Friday with their counterparts from Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt during a meeting initiated by Ankara, a Turkish foreign ministry source told the AFP news agency on Thursday.

Foreign ministers from the so-called E3 group – Britain, France and Germany – will meet counterparts from the newly created R4 group to discuss the Palestinian issue, developments in Yemen and the Strait of Hormuz and ways to end the Russia-Ukraine war, the source said.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will host the meeting, the first to bring together the two groups.

"The seven countries will come together for the first time in the R4+E3 format, at Turkey's initiative," the source said, indicating they would explore "opportunities for cooperation and coordination that could be put into practice ... in the coming period."
In chairing the meeting, Fidan was expected to focus on the international community "increasing pressure on Israel" in response to its the source AFP.

Fidan will also underline support for Saudi Arabia's security in the face of attacks by Yemen's Houthis, and stress the need for permanent freedom of navigation in the Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb Straits.
CBS/AFP
Saudi Aramco reportedly tells staff to evacuate headquarters amid Houthi attacks

Saudi Arabia's state-owned Saudi Aramco, the world's biggest oil company, told staff to evacuate the company's headquarters in the eastern city of Dhahran and to work remotely, the Reuters news agency reported Thursday, citing six sources with knowledge of the matter.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have hit the kingdom repeatedly with missile and drone attacks in recent weeks.

Last week a missile struck an Aramco building in Dhahran, which is on Saudi Arabia's Persian Gulf coast. The strike caused a "limited fire" at Saudi Aramco's headquarters complex, the kingdom's energy ministry said at the time.
Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted a drone over Riyadh
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen's escalating civil war said Thursday that it had intercepted another drone over the Saudi capital Riyadh.
Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki confirmed the interception in a social media post, without offering further details.
Saudi Arabia has been pummeled by Houthi strikes in recent weeks. Experts say geography, missile interceptor shortages and evolving Houthi tactics are helping the Iranian proxy .
Crude oil prices jump as Iran claims to have hit 7 tankers near Strait of Hormuz

World shares and U.S. futures retreated Thursday as oil prices jumped more than 2% following a report by Iran's state television that seven oil tankers were hit by its military or sea mines and damaged near the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf.
If the claim by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps is verified, it would be the largest number of vessels damaged in the Gulf in a single day since the start of the Iran war on Feb. 28.

Brent crude, the international standard, gained 3.2% to hit $112.27 per barrel Thursday. It has been bouncing around $110 in recent days amid uncertainty about when the war with Iran might ease to allow the global energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz to return to normal.
U.S. benchmark crude rose 2.8% to $99.80 per barrel.
In early European trading, Germany's DAX shed 1.1% to 25,367.96, while the CAC 40 in Paris declined 1.3% to 7,816.67. Britain's FTSE 100 was down 0.7% at 10,678.67.
The future for the S&P 500 lost 1% and that for the Dow Jones Industrial Average was 0.7% lower.
CBS/AP
Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it hit 4 vessels transferring oil ship-to-ship in Persian Gulf

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Thursday that it had struck four vessels transferring oil ship-to-ship in the Persian Gulf after they used a route through the Strait of Hormuz that Iran rejects. Ship-to-ship cargo transfers have become more common as tankers and other commercial vessels try to avoid Iranian detection and strikes in the strategic waterway.

In a statement, the IRGC Navy said it "monitored and pursued four violating vessels that had previously passed through an illegal route," referring to shipping lanes in the strait that the Trump administration has encouraged vessels to use to avoid Iranian fees and controls. Tehran considers those southern routes, close to Oman's coast, unauthorized and has targeted vessels trying to use them for months.
"They discovered the vessels transferring oil cargoes from ship to ship in the north-central part of the Persian Gulf," the bulletin read. "All four ships were hit simultaneously and are burning."
The IRGC said three other ships attempting to use routes not recognized by Iran "suffered accidents and caught fire after striking mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, and were brought to a halt."
The IRGC said the U.S. "encouraging vessels to pass through an illegally mined passage has led to an increasing number of maritime incidents day by day."
"If this course continues," the group warned, "the confrontation will extend to the bases of the aggressors in the region."
Saudi authorities raise death toll in attack on airport in eastern city of Dammam to 2
Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said Thursday that the latest attack on the kingdom's airports, a strike on the eastern city of Dammam's King Fahd International Airport, had risen to two.

"The number of deaths resulting from the attack has risen to two, after confirming an additional death. The deceased were a Saudi citizen and a resident of Indian nationality," the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement shared on social media.
It said eight others, "a Saudi citizen, two residents each of Indian, Yemeni, and Bangladeshi nationalities, and a resident of Nepalese nationality," were injured in the attack.

The statement did not assign blame for the attack, but Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen have attacked Saudi airports and other infrastructure for weeks in retaliation for the Saudi government's backing of Yemeni state forces in the neighboring nation's decade-long civil war.

GACA said in its statement that it was continuing work in conjunction with other security authorities "to assess the damages, and to take all necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and employees, and to maintain the security and safety of the civil aviation system in the Kingdom."
Why can't Saudi Arabia stop deadly attacks by Iran's Houthi allies?

Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks have inflicted severe losses on the kingdom and prompted the U.S. to quietly reduce its military footprint in the region as missiles hit energy infrastructure and civilian airports, killing more than 20 people.
Saudi Arabia, despite its size, wealth and a substantial military, has appeared to be on the back foot as it faces the Yemeni rebels.
Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute — far more than any other country in the Middle East, including Israel.
So, why has the kingdom struggled to stop the Houthi barrage? Read .
One killed, 8 injured in Dammam airport attack, Saudis say

An attack targeting the King Fahd International Airport in the eastern Saudi Arabian city of Dammam killed one person and injured eight others Wednesday evening, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said.
The authority said in a statement that injuries from the attack ranged from "minor to serious" and that material damage to the airport was also being assessed.
It did not describe what type of attack occurred, but the kingdom's airports have been targeted repeatedly by projectiles in recent days by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants.
U.S. troops reducing footprint at Middle East posts, sources say

A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official told CBS News on Wednesday the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing regional threats from the Houthis and direct threats from Iran.
NBC News was first to report on the drawdowns.

Asked about the reports, U.S. Central Command spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins told CBS News: "We regularly move U.S. service members and assets to optimize mission readiness. We do not discuss related movements for operational security reasons. U.S. forces remain vigilant and ready to protect American personnel and interests across the region."
The U.S. State Department has also ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia, citing threats posed by the Iran-backed Houthis.
CBS News has learned several U.S. embassies in the Middle East have adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status.
The restricted operations status, which the department introduced in August amid flare-ups in the war with Iran, allows embassies to reduce staffing and services without fully suspending operations.
Debris from intercepted drone kills 2 in Saudi Arabia, energy ministry says
The Saudi energy ministry said that falling debris from the interception of a drone targeting an oil facility killed two people and injured two others on Wednesday.

"The attempted attack resulted in the deaths of two individuals, a Filipino and a Nepali, and injuries to two others," the ministry said in a statement. It did not say who launched the drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field near the UAE border.
State Department orders some U.S. government employees and family members to leave Saudi Arabia
The U.S. has ordered all non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as the kingdom faces escalating attacks by Houthi militants.

"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a social media post Wednesday.

The order came a few days after the , Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and several other countries warned that hostilities could rapidly and without warning spread beyond areas already affected by the fighting.
"The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority, and we will continue to take all necessary steps to protect and support them," Pigott added.
U.S. will suffer "even greater strategic failure" if it chooses war over diplomacy, Iranian FM says
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi issued a warning to the U.S. on Wednesday afternoon, saying it should choose diplomacy over returning to war.

"Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust & reach a just solution," he wrote on X, sharing a link to an opinion piece in the Financial Times. "But if US chooses war over diplomacy, it'll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure."

Araghchi that Iran and the U.S. were still involved in indirect negotiations via mediators over the seven-day ceasefire proposal from September. The proposal was outright rejected by President Trump, but Araghchi said the U.S. was trying to add further clauses to the agreement.
U.S. sanctions Greek law firm for alleged involvement in Iranian "shadow fleet"
The U.S. Treasury announced new sanctions on the Panamanian-Greek law firm Karnakis and Karnakis for involvement in Iran's "shadow fleet" as part of its Operation Economic Outcast.

The U.S. accuses Karnakis and Karnakis of being indirectly involved in Iran's illicit shipping operations for years. A "shadow fleet" refers to oil tankers that hide their true ownership in order to evade sanctions.

"Whether you are conducting illegal oil transfers at sea or sitting in the corner office of a law firm, if you are supporting the Iranian regime, we will find you and sanction you," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "Iran's facilitators must make a choice: Either you are with us or against us. We know who you are, we know what you're doing, and we will continue to take action."

The Treasury also said it sanctioned Singapore- and UAE-based shipping agents, including a fleet of cargo vessels that has directly taken part in Iran's "shadow fleet" and "helped generate substantial revenue for the Iranian regime."
Riyadh airport partially reopens after deadly Houthi strike

A limited number of Saudi airlines took off and landed at the country's main airport on Wednesday, two days after authorities notified airlines that they could resume operations with prior permission.

Saudia and FlyNas were operating flights Wednesday, according to flight-tracking data published by FlightAware. Major carriers, including Lufthansa and Air France, have canceled flights through mid-November.
Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has been hit multiple times this month by Yemen's Houthi rebels and shut down on Oct. 10. A strike two weeks ago killed 13 people and injured hundreds more.
The Houthis have acknowledged attacking the airport, claiming without evidence that Saudi Arabia provided military equipment to government forces through the facility.
Iran criticizes potential Egyptian involvement in Yemen war; Sisi promises only defensive actions
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said any interference in the Yemen war by Egypt or any other country would make the situation "more difficult."
"Egypt has sufficient experience to avoid entangling itself in such a highly complex conflict," said Iran's top diplomat in an interview with Iraqi state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya aired on Tuesday.
"We believe that any foreign presence or interference will only make resolving this issue more difficult," Araghchi noted.

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Wednesday that Cairo's proposed military support for Riyadh was to "defend Saudi territory, and does not include an attack on Yemen," according to a statement from his office.

At a government event titled Egypt Forum 2026, Sisi said the "objective is to defend the kingdom's lands and borders, as well as those of any other Arab state, should it be requested of Egypt," his spokesman said in a statement.
Sisi on Saturday had asked parliament to authorize support for Saudi Arabia in its war with the Houthis, "if requested."
The parliament, which is stacked with supporters of the president, has since held two rare secret sessions, before postponing deliberations until next week.
Iran's new defense minister says first priority is meeting air force needs

Iran's newly appointed defense minister, Mehrdad Akhlaghi, said Wednesday his first hours in office were devoted to meeting the requirements of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Aerospace Force and the army's air defense units.

"We are not in a war of rhetoric in response to repeated threats; we are turning threats into greater readiness and more effective defensive power," he wrote in his first post on X since taking office.
Akhlaghi added Iran was concentrating on its objectives through the use of new technologies.
"We may eat dirt, but we will not give up our soil," he concluded.
Trump blocked Netanyahu's plan for multiday strikes on Iran, report says
President Trump blocked a planned Israeli multiday operation that would have resumed strikes against Iran on the weekend of Oct. 10, according to the Financial Times.

The plan was designed to exceed the intensity of the joint U.S.-Israeli military offensive launched in February, three people familiar with the matter told the paper, and would have struck Iranian nuclear sites, regime targets and civilian infrastructure such as power plants.
The president blocked the strike to avoid escalating conflict before the U.S. midterm elections, according to the report.
Iranian regime needs to be toppled, Netanyahu says
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Wednesday he had directed the Israeli army and intelligence services to topple the Iranian regime.
"The regime in Iran has still not learned the lesson," Netanyahu told a graduation ceremony at an officer training school in the country's southern Negev desert.

"Mojtaba Khamenei, the current tyrant, has decided to follow in his father's footsteps," he said, referring to the country's supreme leader, who replaced his father Ali Khamenei after he was killed in a U.S.-Israeli airstrike on Feb. 28.
"He has taken the safety off, and Iran is once again attempting to develop 'death bombs,'" he added, without giving details on what exactly he was referring to.

"There is only one way to remove this threat once and for all," Netanyahu said, "by toppling the regime in Iran. And that is my directive to the [Israel Defense Forces], the Mossad, and the security services."
He did not expand on how he expected the military or intelligence services to carry out the directive.
Saudi Arabia discusses deployment of up to 10,000 Syrian troops to Yemen

Saudi Arabia has held talks with a senior Syrian military delegation on arrangements to transfer up to 10,000 Syrian fighters to take part in the war against Yemen's Houthi movement, according to a report by the Lebanese Hezbollah-owned Al-Akhbar newspaper, citing Yemeni intelligence sources.

The report claims Syrian military officials visited Saudi Arabia's southern regions of Najran and Asir to inspect sites prepared to receive the fighters, while discussions in Riyadh covered transport logistics, financing and military assignments.

The Syrian delegation included Brig. Gen. Khaled Khattab, former commander of the Ansar al-Tawhid faction and current commander of the 82nd Division in the new Syrian army; and Brig. Gen.Haitham al-Ali, also known as Abu Muslim, commander of the army's Third Corps and a former leader in Hayat Tahrir al-Sham.

Khattab reportedly spent four days in southern Saudi Arabia, accompanied by Saudi officers, visiting sites in the regions of Asir and Najran being prepared to receive Syrian fighters. Meanwhile, al-Ali held several meetings with Saudi officers at the Defense Ministry in Riyadh to discuss the costs of transferring around 10,000 fighters, financial arrangements, additional benefits and their intended military tasks. The delegation reportedly finalized logistical arrangements for the transfer.
The report also raises the possibility that foreign fighters currently in Syria, including Uyghurs, Uzbeks, Tajiks and other nationalities, could be transferred to Yemen.
Iran taps missile industry figure as new defense chief, highlighting focus on weapons production
A missile industry veteran has been tapped as Iran's new defense minister, replacing the previous minister who was killed on Feb. 28, the first day of U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran.
Iranian parliamentarians overwhelmingly approved the appointment of Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi, 68, as the country's new defense chief on Sunday.

Akhlaghi studied chemical engineering at Amirkabir University of Technology and then spent more than four decades working in Iran's military industries, holding senior positions in the Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group, the Aerospace Industries Organization – which has worked on missile development in cooperation with Russia, China and North Korea – and the Defense Industries Organization.
He worked with Hassan Tehrani Moghaddam, a senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander widely regarded as the father of Iran's missile industry.
Akhlaghi has been under international sanctions since 2007 because of his involvement in Iran's missile programs.

His appointment comes as Iran works to rebuild its military facilities and replenish weapons lost during the war. He has pledged to strengthen domestic arms production, and his background suggests rebuilding Iran's missile programs will be a priority for the ministry.

Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia has claimed repeatedly since late August that Iran has rebuilt its weapons manufacturing capacity, including last week, when it said the country was now able to make more arms than "even before it [the war] began."

Early in the war, the it had destroyed more than 85% of Iran's "defense industrial base," and President Trump had Iran's military capabilities were destroyed by U.S. strikes, but experts have questioned that assessment, and Iran has demonstrated an ongoing capacity to launch attacks on ships in the region.
Qatari aircraft leaves Tehran 30 minutes after arrival

A Qatari aircraft arrived in Tehran Tuesday just minutes after a plane carrying Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, departed. The Qatari plane left the Iranian capital approximately 30 minutes later, according to aviation tracking data cited by Iran's semi-official Fars News agency.

The aircraft's short stay raised questions about whether it might have been carrying a diplomatic message amid ongoing indirect negotiations between the U.S. and Iran. Qatar is among the nations that have acted as mediators between the two sides for months.
No information about the aircraft's passengers or why it was in Tehran for only half an hour was provided in the Fars report.
Houthis say they targeted Saudi operations room in Aden, southwest Yemen
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels said they had targeted a Saudi military operations room at Badr Camp in Aden, in southwest Yemen, with a ballistic missile on Wednesday.
Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, in a post on X, called the strike a direct hit.
"Our armed forces successfully targeted the enemy Saudi operations room at Badr Camp in Aden with a ballistic missile. The strike was accurate and direct," he said.
Aden is the de facto seat of power of Yemen's Saudi-backed government, which was forced to decamp after the Houthis occupied the national capital Sanaa more than a decade ago.
The attack claimed by the Houthis Wednesday was the third in a week on Aden.

A police official in Aden told the French news agency AFP earlier that there had been a blast "caused by a Houthi missile." Two other security sources told AFP the strike targeted a site near the city's airport.
Iran threatens undersea internet cables in Strait of Hormuz
A senior official from Iran's Revolutionary Guard threatened to target undersea internet cables in the Strait of Hormuz if Iranian infrastructure comes under attack.

Brig. Gen. Yadollah Javani, the IRGC's deputy for political affairs, warned Iran would use its full capabilities to retaliate if the U.S. and its allies launch new attacks against Iranian infrastructure. He said various investments and assets, including undersea cables carrying internet data in the strategic waterway, could be among the targets of Iranian retaliation if hostilities resume.

"The Americans and their allies have significant investments, and if they want to damage our infrastructure, it is natural that the Islamic Republic will use all its capabilities and easily destroy their investments and assets, including the internet cables that pass beneath the waters of the Strait of Hormuz," he said.
Analysts say cutting the cables in the waterway would most likely affect internet connectivity in Persian Gulf countries.
Iran says Tehran and Washington still engaged in negotiations, ceasefire proposal still in play

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday that Tehran and Washington were still engaged in indirect negotiations via mediators over the seven-day ceasefire proposal presented by Iran in September.
Araghchi said the U.S. was seeking to add further clauses to the Iranian proposal, which Mr. Trump rejected last month.

The proposal called for the end of the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and vessels, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil sales, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the release of frozen Iranian assets.
He said Pakistan and Qatar were among the nations facilitating the indirect talks between Iran and the U.S., as they have been for months.
"The negotiating table remains in place," Araghchi said. "It is the American side that is closing the path, not Iran."
U.S. ramps up warnings to Americans in Middle East after deadly Houthi strikes

U.S. diplomatic missions across the Middle East have issued a new round of security warnings to Americans amid escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants against Saudi Arabia, including an Oct. 10 strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed an American citizen.

The alerts, issued Sunday by U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and several other countries, warned that hostilities could rapidly and without warning spread beyond areas already affected by the fighting. The advisories urged Americans to exercise vigilance and prepare for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions.

"We are actively warning U.S. citizens about the very real threat the Houthis pose and urging them to heed official guidance," Edgar Vasquez, the State Department's deputy assistant secretary for press, told CBS News.

"These alerts are part of a proactive effort by the Trump administration to ensure Americans are aware of potential risks," Vasquez said, adding that the safety and security of American citizens remain the department's "top priority."
Trump says he's deciding how to win Iran war: "We're doing very well with Iran"
President Trump said the U.S. is "doing very well with Iran" and he's just deciding how he wants to win the war.

"As you know, we're doing very well with Iran," Mr. Trump said as he took questions from reporters in the Oval Office at an unrelated executive order signing. "We just have to make a final decision of which way do we want to win? Do we want to win the nice way or the not nice way? But we're doing very well."

The war, which Mr. Trump said would take only a few weeks in March, has now dragged on for almost eight months with no apparent end in sight. Iran said on Tuesday it unless the U.S. drops its sanctions, threats and pressure campaign — an unlikely demand.
The president also discussed Europe not helping the U.S. with the war with Iran, saying, "We don't need any help. But I was testing them."

"I just called individual presidents and prime ministers to ask, would they like to help us? And they said, 'No,'" Mr. Trump said. "I said, 'Well, that's not nice.' You know, we spend hundreds of billions a year on NATO. And they said no."
